content: Omadacycline is indicated for the treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) caused by susceptible microorganisms. It is also indicated for the treatment of acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSIs) caused by susceptible microorganisms. The recommended duration of treatment is 7 to 14 days. Omadacycline has been granted orphan drug designation for the treatment of nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), including pulmonary disease caused by Mycobacterium abscessus complex (MABc). However, its safety and efficacy in patients under 18 years of age have not been established. In clinical trials for CABP, a mortality imbalance was observed. Eight deaths (2%) occurred in patients treated with omadacycline, compared to four deaths (1%) in patients treated with moxifloxacin. The cause of this mortality imbalance remains unknown. All deaths in both treatment groups occurred in patients over 65 years of age, most of whom had multiple comorbidities. The concomitant use of acitretin with omadacycline increases the toxicity of omadacycline through an unknown mechanism and is contraindicated. Oral retinoids used with tetracyclines, including omadacycline, may increase the risk of pseudotumor cerebri (intracranial hypertension). Omadacycline decreases the effects of amoxicillin, ampicillin, dicloxacillin, nafcillin, oxacillin, penicillin G (aqueous, benzathine, procaine), penicillin VK, and piperacillin due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Tetracyclines, including omadacycline, may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. If these agents are used concomitantly, monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of penicillins and consider alternative therapies. Omadacycline increases the effects of atracurium, cisatracurium, pancuronium, rocuronium, succinylcholine, and vecuronium through pharmacodynamic synergism, which may increase the risk of respiratory depression. Avoid or use alternative drugs in such cases. The toxicity of omadacycline is increased when used with bexarotene, isotretinoin, tretinoin, or palovarotene, likely through an unknown mechanism. Avoid or use alternative drugs. Systemic retinoid use has been associated with benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), particularly when used concomitantly with tetracyclines. The coadministration of omadacycline with the cholera vaccine should be avoided due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Systemic antibiotics, including omadacycline, may be active against the vaccine strain, reducing vaccine efficacy. Do not administer the cholera vaccine to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Omadacycline's absorption and efficacy are reduced when coadministered with multivalent cation-containing products, such as aluminum hydroxide, magnesium carbonate, magnesium trisilicate, calcium acetate, calcium carbonate, calcium chloride, calcium citrate, calcium gluconate, calcium/vitamin D, carbonyl iron, ferric carboxymaltose, ferric citrate, or chromium. These agents inhibit gastrointestinal absorption of omadacycline. To avoid chelation and impaired absorption, administer tetracyclines at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after these agents. Modify therapy or monitor closely if coadministration is unavoidable. Similarly, bile acid sequestrants like cholestyramine, colesevelam, and colestipol reduce the levels or effects of omadacycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Monitor for decreased effects of tetracyclines if coadministered with these agents. Separate doses by at least 2 hours to minimize interaction. Ascorbic acid, citric acid/sodium bicarbonate, aspirin/citric acid/sodium bicarbonate, and bismuth-containing products (e.g., bismuth subgallate, bismuth subsalicylate) also decrease the absorption and efficacy of omadacycline. These interactions apply only to the oral forms of both agents. Modify therapy or monitor closely, and separate dosing to avoid reduced absorption.
